utterances.text: And, again, if you could please turn your modesty aside for a moment, just so that we can understand, why were you given this award at this time, in October 2002? Why were you being honoured with this award?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me to explain the positions of another person? I can't give you another answer, but say that my direct superior was probably satisfied with the way I was performing my tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to intend -- I would seek to admit 65 ter 1146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tab 2 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P570, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovski, you described, last week to my colleague Ms. Residovic, how extremely complex the security situation in 2001 was, and so it would be fair to say that it was extremely difficult for you and your colleagues to work from March 2001 to the end of the year. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the members of the Ministry of Interior were extremely pressed with work at that time, and that is with your regular duties and with what you referred to as the additional obligations of the Ministry of Internal Affairs at that time. That statement would be true -- it would be true to say that all of the employees of the Ministry of Interior were extremely pressed during that work, during that period, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that would include those colleagues in the ministry working at high levels of the ministry, persons with large amounts of responsibility. They were also extremely pressed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a very stressful period for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that answer, then, is a yes? Do I take that as a yes?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this would also be true for the minister himself, Mr. Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my learned friend. But for a number of questions already, the witness is expected to testify about the work or the feelings of other individuals. I don't believe this is a proper way of questioning the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness was working at a fairly high level within the Ministry of Interior at that time, and the witness would be able to understand the dynamics in which people were working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would also be true, Mr. Stojanovski, that the minister himself, during that complex time in 2001, would have also been very pressed at work. Right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were in his shoes, probably I would be under a lot of pressure. I would feel under a lot of pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And before we go on, you mentioned these additional obligations of the Ministry of Internal Affairs at that time. What were those additional obligations of the ministry in the spring and summer of 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said "ministry," I was referring to crime police, actually; and I can say that it really had additional duties, primarily with regards to securing, security. Usually, the members of the crime police do not participate in security for protest; but during this time, because of a shortage in personnel or a sufficient number of police officers, it was necessary to have them involved as well in the security activities in relation to protests, regarding facilities of vital importance, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you aware that other units or sectors of the Ministry of Interior, during that difficult period, also had to perform additional obligations or tasks?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is probably so; although, I can't speak of them and their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Stojanovski, would you agree that in exceptional circumstances, times of great pressure and stress, people and institutions don't always follow the strict rules and procedures that they would normally follow during peacetime? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially. You never know in which way will a person react when under threat, when they are in immediate danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whereas, I would not agree with you with regards to the institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although, I could not preclude anything on the basis of the knowledge that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned, during your direct examination, for example, the large numbers of telephone calls that you made and received every day during the crisis time in 2001. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't it, that in 2001, there may have been times of stress when you, for example, instead of taking the time to write an Official Note or a report, you might have reached for your telephone and given a verbal report to your superior. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that such situations existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there may have been times when a particular superior within the Ministry of Interior, instead of drafting written orders and sending them down the chain of command, might have, due to time pressures and stress, have simply issued orders to their subordinates by telephone. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both those cases, when a report is requested or when an order is issued, it can be given orally, but it must be done then followed an order in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But in those times of stress, occasionally times of emergency, people would have a greater tendency to issue orders by telephone, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the previous three questions, as well as this one, are questions of a general nature or asked in a general way. I believe that it would be proper, if my colleague has a specific event in mind, that it would be proper to ask him of this event directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm asking about the general tenure of work the Ministry of Interior in 2001, and how work was done in that complex period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It becomes of very little weight, as you have not established any foundation for this witness's knowledge of others in the ministry and how they worked. You may be on more sure ground asking how this witness worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovski, were there times in 2001, during the crisis time, when, instead of drafting a written order to your -- to any subordinate, you simply reached for the telephone and called that person?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order is not a usual matter in the work of the crime police, because all members of the crime police are under legal duty to carry out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the question in a different way. If there was a task that you wanted performed, were there times in 2001 that you reached for your telephone and directed the appropriate person to carry out that task?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In situations such as those, the task which I assigned or the priority I established was always accompanied with a written document, which was related to a concrete problem that we were working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever assign a task using the telephone during that time?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then what were you doing on all those telephone conversations that you told us about last week? I think you mentioned at least two hours a day you were on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, the unit of internal affairs was -- were obliged to inform me of events that happened on their territory and the measures which they planned to undertake, so as I could enable the head of the sector of internal affairs to carry out his function of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you saying and is it your evidence that you were a mere conduit of information on the telephone, that information went through you up the chain, but instructions were never passed down by you, using the telephone?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I believe I said previously that my instructions were followed with written documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your instructions were followed with written documents. So is it your testimony now that you might have, first, given oral instructions via the telephone or otherwise, and then follow that up with a written document?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the nature of the work requires that measures and activities be taken, or if I receive a written document that we have to carry through, depending on the urgency, it is possible to contact my subordinates by telephone. However, in any event, the written document with my notes later was sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to talk to you a little bit more about your duties during 2001, Mr. Stojanovski. Last week, in response to some questions from my colleague, Ms. Residovic, you explained that: "My duties were to perform the tasks assigned to me by the head of SVR Skopje."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is as page 9083 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then you elaborated. You said your duties were to "facilitate a more efficient and quality executions of the functions of the chief of SVR Skopje," and you said at that time: "My relationship was toward the head, the chief of SVR Skopje, and so were my tasks." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, in the spring and summer of 2001, the head of SVR Skopje was a gentleman named Zoran Efremov. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Zoran Efremov was seriously injured in an automobile accident that summer, which led to him being replaced as head of SVR Skopje in September 2001 by Mr. Kocovski. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim for certain about the reasons due to which Mr. Efremov was replaced; although, there had been other explanations. I have heard also other explanations for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But would it be fair to say that before Mr. Efremov was replaced, you worked with Mr. Efremov fairly closely?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was duty-bound to cooperate with all heads of SVR Skopje, regardless of their name or anything else. I don't understand you. What do you mean by this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- "closely."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Efremov was the chief of SVR Skopje, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you told us earlier that your duty or one of your duties was to "facilitate a more efficient and quality exclusions of the function of chief of SVR Skopje," who was Mr. Efremov, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, in your job, did you have a -- did you have a lot of contact with Mr. Efremov?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you speak to Mr. Efremov on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say, then, that given the very complex security situation at that time, Mr. Efremov had a very difficult and stressful job?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that it was difficult to carry out these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, at page 9084 of the transcript, last week you told us: "I was charged to follow the situation in the OVRs from the point of view of the crime police and to suggest, if necessary, to the head of the SVR certain solutions which could help him carry out his function of coordination." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn now to what is Exhibit 1D107. Your Honours, this would be in the first binder of exhibits that my colleague, Ms. Residovic, provided to you last week at tab 4. You know, I can give -- I can give Mr. Stojanovski my copy of the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see, Mr. Stojanovski, that this is a document that I think you've seen before. It's the "Book of Rules of Organisation and Operation of the Ministry of Internal Affairs." Do you see is that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could turn please to what is Article 9 in this Book of Rules, it's on page 10 of the English version. Do you have Article 9 now, in front of you, Mr. Stojanovski?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see that according to Article -- Article 9 describes the organisation of the sector for internal affairs, the SVR, of the city of Skopje. You see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for example, we see numerous departments and sections, ranging from a duty operating centre, section for defence preparation, organised crime, general crime, drug trafficking, arms trafficking, department for public peace and order, traffic, et cetera, as well as a department for analysis and fire protection. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And below that - this is on the next page in the English version - we see the five OVRs, the departments for internal affairs that were within the area or the organisational unit of the SVR Skopje; Centar, Karpos, Kisela Voda, Gazi Baba, and Cair with their subpolice stations, sectors for operative affairs and analysis. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that the responsibility of SVR Skopje, and, by extension, Zoran Efremov in 2001, was quite large and included numerous departments, sections, police stations, as well as the five separate OVRs. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the framework of the SVR, there are a number of organisational units and this is probably one of the reasons for the existence of my position and that of Mr. Bliznakovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. And so, following up on that point, during that complex summer of 2001, spring/summer 2001, given your competence, your dedication, you made many suggestions to Mr. Efremov about many different aspects of the work of the SVR and of the OVRs, didn't you, in order to assist Mr. Efremov?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, where the crime police was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, no doubt, there were times when Mr. Zoran Efremov, in response to your suggestions, made a decision about a particular task - for example, in a particular OVR - and directed you to relay an instruction to the head of that OVR. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My suggestions were directed towards Mr. Zoran Efremov. In most cases, he personally contacted the heads of the OVRs, if he felt that what I had proposed was correct and justified. However, there were situations when I could, on his behalf, call some of the heads and convey an opinion or an instruction from Mr. Zoran Efremov; that is to say, at the moment, when my proposal or suggestion is conveyed to the sector of the SVR, it is no longer of my ownership. This is now the decision of the head of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in those situations when, on Mr. Efremov's behalf, you called some of the heads of the OVRs and conveyed an opinion or an instruction - perhaps let's focus on instruction from Mr. Efremov - then the heads of the OVRs would have carried out those instructions, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although this happened rarely, they should take them into consideration, the opinions, the suggestions, the understandings, of Mr. Efremov. Mr. Efremov, as head of sector, had a coordination function, among others; and if some of the OVRs requested measures or coordinated activities to be taken in conjunction with another OVR, then if Mr. Efremov agreed with such a proposal, then it was natural that these be carried out by the other OVRs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to clarify, if necessary. There's always one side that requests something, and another side that has to offer something. If an OVR faces a difficulty in its work, SVR Skopje should clarify organisational problems; or, in another case, if an OVR is working on a particular case that requires measures and encompasses the territory of another OVR, then this is conveyed to the relevant OVR, which then has to carry out these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, in other words, I believe, finally, in your response, you clarified that if, for example, Mr. Efremov, as head of SVR Skopje, if he conveys an instruction to a relevant OVR, to a particular OVR, then the members of that OVR have to carry out the instructions of Mr. Efremov. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the relevant OVR, as part of its legal tasks and obligation, requires to undertake measures and activities on a territory of a different OVR, then this instruction is communicated there, where it should be carried out. However, this instruction also is part of the duties and authorisations of the OVR that is requesting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you at all suggesting, in any way, that if the head of an OVR received an instruction from the head of SVR Skopje, the head of the OVR could disregard that instruction? Is that -- are you suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they're not respecting it, they have to explain why they're not carrying out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, in other words, the head of the OVR would have the duty to carry out the instruction of Mr. Efremov, the head of SVR Skopje, or explain why they cannot carry it out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it correct, because these instructions are based in law and for the purpose of carrying out the tasks of the OVR.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In 18:12 [sic], instead of "that is requesting this," it is "of which it is requested." That is, line 55:18.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe you mentioned, a few minutes ago, that there were some times in 2001 when Mr. Efremov directed you to relay an instruction, for example, to the head of an OVR. In that sense, would it be fair to say that, during 2001, part of your function was to be sort of an extension of Mr. Efremov?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's fair to say that. I was superior to organisational units, which I hope I was successful in explaining, specialised or especially equipped for carrying out certain tasks. If an OVR had the need of these units, it would turn to the head of the SVR; and then the head of the SVR could turn to me and ask of me to organise this with the organisational units which were subordinate to me. In such cases, and in this many shall, if this is how you understand an extension, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And particularly, during that stressful period, during 2001, if the head of an OVR needed to speak with Zoran Efremov but could not reach Zoran Efremov on the telephone, the head of that OVR might call you, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My work was not to -- to be a substitute of Mr. Efremov, but it did happen that certain heads of OVRs would call him and ask for advice related to criminalistic affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand that, but my question is something different. During those stressful periods during 2001, there were times, weren't there, when, for whatever reason, instead of calling Mr. Efremov to convey some information or to seek assistance, a head of an OVR might have called you, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you had also mentioned, if -- during your direct examination, I believe you mentioned that if members of the Ministry of Interior who are assigned to a particular OVR did not perform their duties in accordance with the law, then their superior, the head of the OVR, would need to raise the issue of their disciplinary responsibility. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know enough about this area, but I could clarify how this happened in practice. If, for example, if one employee at an OVR, for example, oversteps or does not carry out -- oversteps discipline or does not carry out measures, then the head of the OVR is due to document this case and to give it to the head of the sector for internal affairs, Skopje, who then proposes -- issues a proposal for establishing disciplinary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojanovski, suppose the head of the OVR does not perform his duties, or her duties, in accordance with the law or the regulations of the ministry, who would have the duty, then, to address the disciplinary responsibility of the head of the OVR?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be his immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for example, the immediate superior of the head of OVR Cair, in 2001, who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the sector for internal affairs. In 2001 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That would have been Mr. Efremov then, the head of the SVR Skopje.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2001, to avoid any misunderstanding, in 2001, many persons -- several persons carried out the duty of head of SVR. If we're talking about the period when Mr. Efremov was appointed or head of this sector, yes. But, once again, there is not linked to a name; rather, it is linked to a job position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. That makes perfect sense. Thank you for that. So the head of the SVR, then, retains some disciplinary powers over the head of the OVR, right?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is not something I've worked on. But I know that there are decisions for establishing disciplinary commissions. I think this was a transferred authorisation of the minister. Since I did not work on matters such as these, I leave room for -- for the possibility that this not -- may not exactly be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But you've already explained that the head of the SVR would have the responsibility to address the disciplinary issue for the head of an OVR. That means, doesn't it, that the OVRs, as an organisational unit of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, are not fully independent of the SVRs, are they?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe these are viewpoints, whether control and execution of tasks is mixed, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if you in your work today have the ability to initiate disciplinary proposals against one of your -- against a member of your unit or section, that person would not be independent of you, would he?

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person must implement the law, enforce the law, and carry out work tasks. When we say "independent," this does not mean independent of the law and legal obligations. If one establishes that this is not being respected, then it's another viewpoint now. This is not a matter of independence of work, but an aspect of supervision or something like that. But could I not link what you are saying, in terms of independence and disciplinary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would mean -- if I'm allowed to interpret in a more free manner, ultimately this means that an order could issued that a person be brought in. OVR will carry out this task independently, and this is where independence comes in. If it does not act upon this order, then we have an altogether different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, if I with paraphrase what you're explaining then, when you use the term "independent" to describe the OVRs during your direct examination, you meant that members of the OVR have a certain independence in terms of their ability to carry out tasks, but you were not suggesting that OVRs were independent and outside the normal chain of command of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're obligated by the Book of Rules, if this is what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETRE STOJANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this forms a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. Shall we break at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. I was waiting until you reached a logical point. We adjourn now, to resume tomorrow at 9.00, and I won't say anything about the progress of this case, this witness. We resume again at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
